author: Nick Ackerman
title: Closed-End Funds: Top 10 Performers For 2018
text:
As 2018 comes to an end in only a few short weeks it seems like now might be a good time to see what had been working for 2018. This includes funds that are in varied sectors such as; healthcare, multi-sector bonds, high yield, and even a utility concentrated fund. At this point in the year, there are a total of 359 funds that have a negative NAV return, while 145 funds have a positive NAV return. This is further narrowed when looking at funds with $300 million or more in assets to just 72 funds performing positively and 146 funds showing a negative total NAV return for the year. The purpose of only focusing on the funds that have a higher market cap is due to the additional risks that an investor may face with smaller CEFs, this could include higher fees and generally lower trading volume.
It's not really too shocking that there are more under performing CEFs at this point, as the broader market has taken a dive due to U.S.-China trade uncertainties and lower expectations for global growth going into 2019. These two factors have done much to dent the enthusiasm for the longest bull market in U.S. history. The ETF that is generally used to track the broader market, SPDR S&P 500 ( SPY ) has been flirting back and forth for the last couple months with positive and negative returns for the year. SPY currently sits at a market return of 0.78%, with a NAV return of 0.90%.
SPY data by YCharts
I chose to focus on the total NAV return for CEFs, as CEFs can vary greatly between their market price and NAV price. But I firmly believe that the more important part is what the NAV is doing once you own shares in a CEF. The market price is only merely important when buying and selling the fund. So, with that being said, the list is in order from lowest to highest according to total NAV return YTD.
BlackRock Science and Technology Trust ( BST ) This fund is showing a return of 5.10% NAV YTD, the market price has an even more impressive return of 15.90%! There are several factors that I believe that has lead to such an enthusiastic market price increase. First of all, the fund had a distribution increase this year, in fact, the fund had two increases just last year as well. The fund started out with a distribution at inception of $0.10 and is now currently paying out $0.15 per share per month. As CEF investors are generally those who are looking for higher than usual income, you can't go wrong with a fund that is increasing that income. The fund currently sits at a yield of 6.12% market yield and 6.49% NAV yield.
It may not be too surprising why this fund has done well, as this fund states their investment approach of "invest at least 80% of its total assets in equity securities issued by U.S. and non-U.S. science and technology companies in any market capitalization range, selected for their rapid and sustainable growth potential from the development, advancement and use of science and/or technology." They are invested primarily in big tech names, even with the beatings they have taken recently it doesn't appear to have hurt BST too much at this time.The top three holdings include Microsoft Corp ( MSFT ), Amazon Inc ( AMZN ), and Apple Inc ( AAPL ). These are household names and need no further introductions at this point. BST will also utilize an option writing strategy on a portion of the equities in its portfolio.
BST should perform well going forward if the global economy does not completely shut down going into 2019.
Source - CEFconnect
Pimco Dynamic Credit and Mortgage Income Fund ( PCI ) PCI is quite the popular fund here on Seeking Alpha, and one of my favorites too. The fund is showing positive NAV performance this year at 5.22%, with an even greater market return of 9.30%. The surprising part is that this fund is actually still trading at a discount of 1.31% at the time of writing this. The fund has been being kicked back and forth between premium and discount for a good portion of this year. Many of the Pimco funds do trade at premiums and I didn't expect to see this fund return back to a discount for quite some time.
The fund states they "will normally invest at least 80% of its net assets in a portfolio of mortgage-related securities and other debt instruments of varying maturities. The fund will normally invest at least 25% of its total assets in privately issued mortgage-related securities." With that being said, the fund owns a lot of the "other debt instruments" in their portfolio, making them qualify as a multi-sector bond fund. This gives the managers quite the broad range of securities they are able to invest assets into.
This fund is owned by a lot of CEF investors and is quite well known in the Seeking Alpha community, thankfully, the fund has been able to show a positive performance while so many funds this year have struggled. Pimco knows what they are doing as bond managers, I think they will continue to show strong performance going forward.
Source - CEFconnect
Eaton Vance Enhanced Equity Income Fund II ( EOS ) EOS is another fund that I really like and owned. The fund is showing a YTD NAV return of 5.28%, with a similar market return of 5.09%. The fund trades at a discount of 3.70%, which isn't typical for this fund in 2018, only showing a discount earlier in the year and the last couple of months.
The fund states their strategy as "investing in a portfolio of primarily large- and mid-cap securities that the investment advisor believes have above-average growth and financial strength and writes call options on individual securities to generate current earnings from the option premium." This gives the managers a very flexible investing policy. The fund is currently heavily weighted in the tech sector, their top ten holdings include names like Amazon Inc ( AMZN ), Alphabet Inc ( GOOG ), and Microsoft Corp ( MSFT ) to name a few.
Similarly to BST above, this fund would be for a bullish investor that believes we can have a strong 2019 global economy.
Source - CEFconnect
Duff & Phelps Select Income Fund Inc ( DNP ) This is a fund that surprised me, as a fund invested heavily in utilities at 67.9% and oil & gas sector at 18.5%, I was surprised the fund has done so well. DNP has delivered a YTD NAV return of 5.81%, with a market return of 8.82%. This is a fund that defines consistency though, as far as its distribution is concerned. How about the same $0.065 monthly payout since 1997, I'm not too familiar with too many funds that can say the same. That's a big positive, however, the downside to this is the fund is trading at a premium of 15.24% and typically does not come close to a discount or even par for that matter except on extreme sell-offs.
DNP states achieving their objectives by "investing primarily in a diversified portfolio of equity and fixed income securities of companies in the public utilities industry." This gives them a defensive tilt, which makes me surprised they have been able to perform this year with other tech names. The oil & gas exposure is also a surprise that they've been able to manage this return as well.
For how good the fund is, I just can't seem to push myself to paying such a large premium. I am holding off any purchases until potentially a bear market turns up and I can purchase the shares closer to par.
Source - CEFconnect
Tekla World Healthcare Fund ( THW ) This is a fund I've just recently covered and readers that follow me know that I like and have liked for most of 2018. The fund is showing a NAV return of 5.85% and a market return of 3.91% for the year. THW is showing a deep discount of 9.63%, and does generally trade at a wide discount but I don't think it is necessarily deserved. The fund does have a high yield of 10.90%, with a NAV yield of 9.85%, which does deserve its own word of caution as a higher yield is harder for the fund to maintain over time.
The fund holds many big healthcare names, with a global focus. The fund states their as "a versatile growth and income investment strategy investing across all healthcare sub-sectors and across a company's full capital structure. THW places an emphasis on innovative healthcare companies worldwide and invests at least 40% of managed assets in non-U.S. companies." This provides the managers great flexibility in choosing equities, preferred, and fixed income holdings within the healthcare sector.
I believe THW can continue to perform, even going into 2019. But, a couple of risks include the higher yield of almost 10% on the NAV and the uncertainty that new healthcare regulations may have a negative effect on their underlying holdings. The one thing I like about healthcare is the fact that it doesn't appear to follow the broader market so much, instead, paving its own trail through bull and bear markets depending on new regulations that may be presented.
Source - CEFconnect
Pimco Dynamic Income Fund ( PDI ) PDI shares many similarities with its larger PCI counterpart. PDI is up 6.02% on a NAV basis and is showing a market return of a whopping 12.80%. This fund is one of those Pimco funds that stays at premiums for long periods of time, at this time its no exception, with a premium of 11.54%. PDI is slightly older than PCI, coming out about 6 months earlier with an inception date of 5/25/2012.
The fund has a very similar strategy as PCI as "normally invests worldwide in a portfolio of debt obligations and other income-producing securities of any type and credit quality, with varying maturities and related derivative instruments." They continue with "normally invest at least 25% of its total assets in privately issued mortgage related securities." Again, this gives the Pimco managers great flexibility in what they believe may be presenting the most opportunity at the time of deploying cash for investments.
The large premium turns me off of PDI, but that's where PCI can come in handy. The funds are very similar at this point and I believe that PCI is the place to be when purchasing fixed income assets managed by Pimco. So I would prefer personally putting any investment money to work in PCI at this time.
Source - CEFconnect
Barings Corporate Investors ( MCI ) I have to admit MCI has never crossed my radar before, with an inception date of 9/1/1971, this fund has been around for a while. So far in 2018 it has shown quite the NAV return, coming in at 6.57% and a market return of 4.56%. The fund does trade at a slight discount of 1.70%, though, with a sporadic history of jumping between a discount and premium throughout the year. This fund is unique in that they only report the NAV on a quarterly basis, this can lead some investors away as they are kind of not being able to know on a daily basis what the NAV is doing. This can cause confusion as to what the true premium and discount is. The fund also pays on a quarterly schedule, further pushing some income investors away.
They state their strategy as "invests principally in privately placed, below-investment grade, long-term debt obligations and often accompanied by equity features, purchased directly from their issuers and sourced through Barings extensive deal network of private equity sponsors." This helps explain why the NAV is only updated on a quarterly basis, it is hard to come up with a value on privately placed investments so trying to produce a NAV everyday is not viable.
With the hard to place value and riskier high-yield assets, investors may want to be cautious with an investment in MCI. For an investor that is a little bit more aggressive then this fund may be for you. The fund has performed well so far in 2018 but is hard to put a prediction on for 2019.
Source - CEFconnect
Tekla Healthcare Opportunities Fund ( THQ ) THQ is another fund I've recently covered and have been a fan of for most of 2018. So far it hasn't steered me wrong, with a NAV return of 9.88% and a market return of 9.80%. The fund shares a lot of similarities with THW, except with no emphasis on holdings globally. The fund shares a similar deep discount of 9.81%, and is also plagued with being at this discount almost perpetually. The fund has a more reasonable distribution rate of 7.53% and NAV distribution rate of a very reasonable 6.79%.
The fund states their strategy as "versatile growth and income investment strategy investing across all healthcare sub-sectors and across a company's full capital structure." Exactly the same as THW but without the global emphasis like I mentioned above.
THQ is similarly dependent upon new regulations that may be introduced going into 2019 and is really at the mercy of those changes in healthcare going forward. I believe the fund offers a sustainable distribution and at a deep discount I am liking the opportunity that THQ has going forward.
Source - CEFconnect
Eagle Point Credit Company LLC ( ECC ) ECC is another quite unique fund on this list, as they give an estimated monthly NAV per share amount, this range is in the 10 cent range. With that being said, CEFconnect is showing a NAV return of 10.23% for the year and a market decline of 6.01% (as of writing this fund has gone ex-div today as well and is down 6.79% for the day.) The fund is showing a discount of 4.39%, which isn't typical as the fund generally trades at a premium. The fund also has a whopping 15.31% distribution rate and a NAV rate of 14.63%.
To help explain why the fund only gives monthly estimates they describe their investment approach as "investing primarily in equity and junior debt tranches of collateralized loan obligations (CLOs). The CLOs in which we invest are collateralized by a diverse portfolio consisting primarily of below investment grade U.S. senior secured loans." This type of investment is best described by Investopedia as " A collateralized loan obligation (CLO) is a security backed by a pool of debt, often low-rated corporate loans. Collateralized loan obligations are similar to collateralized mortgage obligations (CMO), except that the underlying loans are of a different type and character. With a CLO, the investor receives scheduled debt payments from the underlying loans, assuming most of the risk in the event borrowers default. In return for taking on the default risk, the investor is offered greater diversity and the potential for higher-than-average returns."
There are considerable risks in these types of holdings and I don't believe they are for everyone, especially a person who may not be expecting to have a great economy going into 2019. The fact that the fund does offer a steep discount that isn't typical, does draw some interest as well as ECC offering a monthly distribution of $0.20 or a 15.31% rate.
Source - CEFconnect
BlackRock Health Sciences Trust ( BME ) BME has been having a terrific year, as this fund has shown the highest total NAV return for CEFs of $300 million in assets or more. The fund is up 12.85%, with a market return of 16.45%. The fund has propelled itself to a premium of 5.48% as investors have bid up the shares through 2018. The fund has an attractive distribution rate of 5.99% though, paid at a monthly rate of $0.20 per share.
The fund states their strategy as "at least 80% of its assets in equity securities of companies engaged in the health sciences and related industries and equity derivatives with exposure to the health sciences industry. The trust utilizes an option writing strategy to enhance dividend yield." The company invests in primarily healthcare equipment makers and in biotech companies, with the top three holdings currently United Health Group Inc ( UNH ), Pfizer Inc ( PFE ), and Abbott Laboratories ( ABT ). This is followed by other large healthcare names like Merck & Co Inc ( MRK ) and Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ). The company being able to strike up the right holdings throughout the year and utilizing their option strategy has been able to provide these spectacular returns.
Whatever they're doing, we want them to continue because its working and has made investors quite the profit this year. Being invested in the healthcare industry does rely on an investor being conscious of the fact that new regulations can effect this CEFs holdings greatly, and in turn, effect the returns going forward for BME. This is similar to THQ and THW above, though, I believe BME can continue to perform well going into 2019 even with this fact. Even if BME doesn't manage to show quite the same performance next year, investors are paid a generous 6% distribution. The real drawback of the fund here is the premium that exists in the fund at this time, an investor may be more comfortable waiting for a discount in the fund.
Source - CEFconnect
Conclusion With 2019 a few short weeks away, I thought it was a good time to review what had worked for 2018 and see if they still sound like a good way to head into 2019.
It would appear that the healthcare sector has had quite the year, this is in contrast to the sector struggling in 2016. Using the Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund ( XLV ) as a barometer, the ETF was down -2.83% in that year. Then 2017 was strong for XLV as well with a return of 21.70% and it appears that good fortune has continued into 2018.
But after that, there doesn't seem to be a strong correlation with another specific sector performing well when looking at CEFs, more of a mixture of sectors and strategies.
